question: Can a pretrained video diffusion model edit the object, camera, or temporal motion of an existing video from sparse source-to-target point trajectories while preserving content that appears anywhere in the input, rather than regenerating from only its first frame?

key_findings.claim: MotionV2V represents an edit as the difference between tracked source trajectories and user-specified target trajectories, conditioning a frozen video generator on the complete source video and three rasterized correspondence channels.
key_findings.evidence: The method tracks points through the source, lets a user change their positions and visibility over time, and renders colored Gaussian blobs with standard deviation 10 pixels into source-trajectory, source-background, and target-trajectory control videos. A control branch duplicated from the first 18 CogVideoX-5B transformer blocks injects zero-initialized residuals into the frozen main branch; its patchifier accepts 48 channels formed by three 16-channel latent control tensors.

key_findings.claim: The central training-data contribution is a counterfactual pairing pipeline, but its claimed identity of content is an approximation rather than a guaranteed invariant.
key_findings.evidence: A real contiguous clip supplies the target. A counterfactual source is produced using diffusion-based frame interpolation between randomly selected endpoints with an LLM-written prompt, temporal resampling between random endpoints including reversal, and geometric crop/rotation/scale transforms; TAPNext then extracts point tracks. Only endpoints are anchored during generative interpolation, so interiors can change appearance, identity, geometry, or events, and geometric transforms deliberately alter pixels. The pairs are plausibly more content-aligned than unrelated videos, but not literally identical-content supervision.

anchors.section: 3.3 Frame interpolation, temporal resampling, and spatial transformation

key_findings.claim: A 41-participant preference study strongly favors MotionV2V on 20 hand-created edits, but the aggregation omits uncertainty and participant-level design details.
key_findings.evidence: For each edit, participants chose the best of MotionV2V, ATI, ReVideo, and Go-with-the-Flow. MotionV2V receives 70% of content-preservation choices, 71% of motion-accuracy choices, and 69% of overall-quality choices; ATI receives 24%, 24%, and 25%, ReVideo 1%, 2%, and 1%, and Go-with-the-Flow 5%, 3%, and 5%. The paper does not report confidence intervals, per-participant or per-clip distributions, significance tests, randomization/order, rater expertise, tie handling, or inter-rater agreement.

key_findings.claim: On a 100-video reconstruction-style benchmark, MotionV2V reports the best L2, SSIM, and LPIPS values, but the construction of the evaluated source-target pair is internally inconsistent in the text.
key_findings.evidence: The reported values are L2 0.024, SSIM 0.098, and LPIPS 0.031, versus ATI 0.038/0.094/0.072, Go-with-the-Flow 0.067/0.089/0.088, and ReVideo 0.096/0.080/0.106. Section 4.3 says a video is split into first half V0 and second half V1, V1 is reversed to V1-prime, and then says the last frame of V0 matches the first of V1-prime; for ordinary chronological halves that equality does not follow. It next says V0 is input and V1 the target, while the supplement and Figure 8 only say one half is reversed to create common starting frames. Whether V0, V1, or V1-prime is reversed and which pair is scored is therefore unresolved.

key_findings.claim: The quantitative comparison structurally advantages full-video conditioning and therefore does not isolate the proposed architecture or counterfactual supervision from input-information access.
key_findings.evidence: The 100 internet videos are explicitly selected so significant content appears mid-video but not in the first frame. MotionV2V receives the full source video, whereas ATI, ReVideo, and the adapted Go-with-the-Flow receive only the first frame with their respective controls. Better preservation of later-appearing content is an expected consequence of observing that content. The experiment establishes the value of full-video access for this constructed setting, not that MotionV2V is intrinsically better under matched observations.

key_findings.claim: The baseline adaptations differ in backbone, prompting, spatial masks, and motion representation, leaving several simultaneous confounds in the headline comparison.
key_findings.evidence: ATI uses Wan2.1 image-to-video with a first frame, target tracks, and a prompt; ReVideo uses Stable Video Diffusion without a prompt and, because masks are unavailable for these edits, exposes the full frame as editable; Go-with-the-Flow is reimplemented with Wan2.2 rather than its original CogVideoX and converts rasterized target tracks through RAFT to flow/noise. MotionV2V uses CogVideoX-5B, the full video, source and target tracks, and three latent controls. These are task-interface comparisons, not controlled component ablations.

key_findings.claim: The model has a documented correspondence-capacity ceiling: conditioning on too many points causes it to stop following all requested trajectories.
key_findings.evidence: The implementation uses approximately 20 point trajectories at inference because the authors observe failure when too many points are provided. No capacity curve, threshold distribution, or dependence on occlusion, object count, video resolution, or motion magnitude is measured, so the practical ceiling is only qualitatively characterized.

key_findings.claim: Exact copied trajectories can create duplicate-object or identity-copy artifacts, and random two-pixel jitter is a heuristic mitigation rather than a demonstrated general solution.
key_findings.evidence: The supplement shows that reusing the basketball's exact original track can prompt the model to reproduce a second basketball; adding independent plus-or-minus two-pixel noise to each target point reduces the artifact in the displayed example. The paper provides no quantitative jitter ablation, distributional study, or analysis of whether jitter degrades precise edits.

anchors.section: 10 Importance of Random Motion Jitter and Figure 9

key_findings.claim: Iterative editing extends the interface compositionally, but the exhibited sequence accumulates subject drift and does not support the suggestion of indefinitely repeatable editing.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 6 applies five sequential trajectory edits to the same clip and the text suggests editing can continue 'infinitely.' The accompanying result visibly changes the person and scene over iterations, and the limitations section acknowledges quality degradation under large edits. There is no identity, drift, or perceptual-quality curve versus iteration count.

key_findings.claim: The qualitative suite demonstrates a broad interface—arbitrary-time object motion, camera changes, and time reversal—but only through eight selected short examples without a benchmark or failure denominator.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 shows eight hand-designed edits including moving a horse, basketball, person, water stream, and waterfall; altering camera zoom/pan; and reversing motion. Figure 5 contrasts editing from first versus later timestamps. These examples support capability existence, but the paper gives no sampling protocol, total attempt count, edit-magnitude strata, source license/domain breakdown, or systematic success criterion.

key_findings.claim: The training recipe is unusually concrete about scale and hardware but not reproducible from public ingredients.
key_findings.evidence: The model is trained from CogVideoX-5B on 100,000 counterfactual pairs derived from an internal pool of 500,000 videos, using 49 frames at 480x720, batch size 32, 15,000 iterations, learning rate 1e-4, L2 latent diffusion loss, and eight H100 GPUs for one week. The internal videos, generated pairs, prompt generation details, filters, and sampling code are not released or characterized sufficiently to reconstruct the data distribution.

key_findings.claim: No ablation establishes which proposed ingredients cause the reported gains.
key_findings.evidence: The paper does not remove full-video conditioning, source trajectories, source-background control, target control, visibility encoding, track dropout, frame-interpolation pairs, temporal resampling, geometric transforms, frozen-main-branch training, the 18-block control depth, or inference jitter. Consequently, the contribution of counterfactual data versus architecture versus simply exposing the full source remains unidentified.

method.core_idea: Turn sparse trajectory displacement into a video-to-video control signal: preserve the full source clip as appearance and scene context, rasterize source and desired tracks into aligned control videos, and train only a copied control branch using synthetic counterfactual pairs whose content is intended to match while motion differs.
method.mechanism: TAPNext tracks source points and visibility. Each track is assigned a color and rendered as a Gaussian blob in source-foreground, source-background, and target control videos. A modified patchifier encodes their latents; 18 copied CogVideoX-5B transformer blocks process the controls and inject zero-initialized residuals into a frozen 30-block main generator conditioned on the full source. Training targets real clips while inputs are interpolation-, time-resampling-, or geometry-modified counterfactuals. At inference, users edit about 20 trajectories through clicks, automatic tracking, and Bezier interpolation, with small random jitter added to discourage literal object copying.
assumptions: Sparse 2D correspondences adequately specify the intended object, camera, and temporal edit without explicit depth, masks, segmentation, or 3D scene structure.
TAPNext produces identity-consistent tracks and reliable visibility labels through occlusion and deformation.
Per-track colors and overlapping Gaussian blobs remain distinguishable at the selected point density and resolution.
A generatively interpolated or geometrically transformed clip retains enough content identity with its target to serve as counterfactual supervision.
The model learns motion displacement rather than shortcuts from interpolation artifacts, LLM prompts, transform signatures, or data-source biases.
The frozen CogVideoX-5B prior contains the appearance, physics, and editing capacity needed for unseen objects and motions.
A control branch copied from the first 18 blocks is sufficient and its zero-initialized injections do not destabilize source preservation.
Approximately 20 user-visible point tracks are adequate for practical editing despite the admitted high-point-count failure.
Independent plus-or-minus two-pixel jitter breaks identity-copy shortcuts without materially changing requested motion precision.
Short 49-frame, 480x720 training clips transfer to the range of duration, resolution, occlusion, and camera motion implied by the broad claims.
Comparisons against first-frame methods remain informative even when MotionV2V uniquely observes content appearing later in the video.
The ambiguous reversed-half construction was implemented in an internally coherent way even though the written protocol does not identify it unambiguously.

techniques.role: Expresses a motion edit as correspondence-level displacement and visibility changes rather than a text prompt or dense optical flow.
Uses TAPNext to generate source trajectories for training and automatic point propagation in the interface.
Maps sparse correspondences into temporally aligned image-like controls with track identity encoded by color.
Separates source foreground tracks, source background, and desired target tracks into three latent control videos.
Retains the pretrained video prior while limiting trainable parameters to the control pathway.
Adds control-branch residuals gradually from an initially neutral mapping.
Creates alternative interior motion between endpoints using a diffusion interpolator and generated prompt.
Changes speed and direction while retaining sampled visual content.
Creates crop, rotation, and scale motion differences without separately labeled edited videos.
Subsamples tracked points to diversify conditioning density during training.
Interpolates user-selected keypoints into editable target trajectories.
Perturbs target tracks at inference to reduce literal duplication induced by exact trajectory reuse.

evaluations.setting: 41-person user study over 20 manually created trajectory edits, with all four method outputs presented for best-result selection.
evaluations.metric: Fraction of choices for content preservation, motion accuracy, and overall quality; no confidence intervals or participant/clip-level inferential statistics are reported.
evaluations.result: MotionV2V receives 70%, 71%, and 69%; ATI 24%, 24%, and 25%; ReVideo 1%, 2%, and 1%; Go-with-the-Flow 5%, 3%, and 5%.
evaluations.baseline: ATI on Wan2.1, ReVideo on Stable Video Diffusion, and adapted Go-with-the-Flow on Wan2.2, with materially different inputs and control interfaces.

evaluations.setting: 100 selected internet videos in which important content appears after the first frame; a half-video reversal protocol is described inconsistently between the main text and supplement.
evaluations.metric: Pixel L2, SSIM, and LPIPS against the held-out/reversed half, with no uncertainty, seeds, sample-level breakdown, or significance tests.
evaluations.baseline: First-frame-conditioned ATI, ReVideo, and Go-with-the-Flow; only MotionV2V receives the full source video, confounding preservation with observation access.

evaluations.setting: Eight selected short videos with object, camera, time-reversal, and arbitrary-start-time edits.
evaluations.metric: Visual examples only; no defined success score, attempt denominator, blind rating, or benchmark strata.
evaluations.result: The examples show plausible relocation of several objects, camera zoom/pan, motion reversal, and edits initiated after frame one, with occasional deformation or drift visible in difficult cases.
evaluations.baseline: Side-by-side outputs from ATI, ReVideo, and Go-with-the-Flow on selected cases, plus source and trajectory overlays.

evaluations.setting: Five sequential edits applied iteratively to one source clip.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative persistence of motion controllability and visual identity across iteration count.
evaluations.result: The requested changes remain visually expressible, but subject and scene appearance drift; no quantitative curve supports indefinite repeated editing.
evaluations.baseline: The original video and intermediate generations; no one-shot composite-edit or identity-preserving baseline.

evaluations.setting: One supplemental basketball example comparing exact target tracks with independent plus-or-minus two-pixel jitter.
evaluations.result: Exact tracks produce a second basketball in the shown case; jitter suppresses the duplicate in the displayed output.
evaluations.baseline: The same model and edit without trajectory jitter; no multi-example or precision-cost analysis.

evaluations.metric: Data volume, optimization steps, and accelerator time.
evaluations.result: 100,000 counterfactual pairs sampled from 500,000 internal videos; batch 32, 15,000 iterations, learning rate 1e-4, eight H100s for one week.
evaluations.baseline: No compute-, parameter-, data-, or wall-clock-matched training baseline and no reported inference latency.

limitations: Author-stated: the model fails to follow every trajectory when too many point controls are supplied, motivating an informal limit of about 20 points.
Author-stated: sufficiently large motion changes can reduce generation quality and content preservation.
The 100-video quantitative protocol is internally inconsistent about which half is reversed and which source-target pair is scored, preventing exact reconstruction from the paper alone.
Only MotionV2V observes the entire input video; baselines observe the first frame, and the test set is selected specifically for content absent from that frame.

Backbones and control channels differ across all baselines, so the reported gaps do not isolate full-video conditioning, the control architecture, trajectory representation, training data, or base-model quality.
The counterfactual pairs do not guarantee identical content because a generative interpolator synthesizes unconstrained interior frames and geometric transforms change pixel content.
No ablation measures the contributions of interpolation, temporal, and spatial pair generation or of each of the three control videos.
No ablation compares full-video versus first-frame conditioning within MotionV2V or evaluates a matched-information baseline.
No quantitative study measures the point-count ceiling, track density, occlusion, trajectory overlap, motion magnitude, or visibility-edit difficulty.
The internal 500,000-video pool, 100,000 derived pairs, prompt generator, and preprocessing/filtering details are unavailable, limiting reproducibility and distributional audit.
Evaluation uses only 49-frame clips and does not test long videos, high-resolution transfer, long occlusions, shot changes, or out-of-distribution frame rates.
The 41-person study lacks confidence intervals, per-rater/per-clip results, assignment and ordering details, tie handling, expertise, agreement, and significance testing.
The metric study reports no uncertainty, seed variation, sample-level outcomes, metric implementation details, or stratification; the unusually small absolute SSIM values are not explained.
Qualitative evidence consists of selected examples without an attempt denominator or failure taxonomy, so broad claims about editing any object in general scenes are not prevalence estimates.
Tracking errors and the time, skill, and number of corrections required from users are not evaluated.
No runtime, memory, or latency is reported for tracking, user interaction, or generation, and no comparison is compute-matched.
The method uses 2D correspondences without explicit depth or occlusion geometry, which can make crossing tracks, camera-object ambiguity, and disocclusion underdetermined.
The paper does not report a public implementation, model weights, training pairs, evaluation videos, or exact benchmark manifests in the pinned version.
failure_modes: Too many trajectory controls cause some requested paths to be ignored.
Large displacements or motion edits can deform subjects, change appearance, or reduce source-content preservation.
Reusing an exact source trajectory can trigger literal identity copying and duplicate an object; the shown basketball artifact motivates random jitter.
Repeated generation compounds model error and produces visible subject or scene drift across iterative edits.
Incorrect TAPNext correspondence or visibility predictions can attach a target path to the wrong object or propagate an error through time.
Sparse 2D points can underspecify rotation, articulation, depth ordering, scale change, occlusion, or the spatial extent of the object to move.
Overlapping colored Gaussian tracks or similar track colors can blur point identity at high density.
A target path that demands unseen background or object surfaces can force hallucination rather than faithful editing.
Counterfactual-generation artifacts can become shortcuts during training, reducing transfer to authentic user edits.
First-frame baselines can appear to lose content simply because the selected source content is never supplied to them.
reusable_insights: For video editing, condition on the entire source whenever preserving later-emerging objects matters; then compare against baselines with the same observation budget.
Represent an edit relationally as source-to-target correspondence change rather than target motion alone, so the model can distinguish preservation from displacement.
Counterfactual supervision can turn unlabeled video into edit pairs, but content invariance should be measured rather than assumed.
Separate source foreground, source background, and desired target motion when their semantic roles differ, then ablate each channel to verify the factorization.
Zero-initialized residual injection into a frozen generative backbone is a practical way to add controls without immediately disrupting a pretrained prior.
Visibility is part of trajectory control: point absence can encode occlusion or temporal extent without a separate binary tensor.
Exact conditioning signals may leak a copy shortcut; tiny randomized perturbations are a useful diagnostic, but their accuracy tradeoff needs a sweep.
Evaluation for editing should cross information access, edit magnitude, point density, occlusion, source-time position, and object count instead of reporting a single aggregate.
A reconstruction benchmark should publish an executable transformation from original video to source and target, especially when reversal and indexing determine the ground truth.
Iterative-edit claims require drift-versus-iteration curves and comparison with one-shot composite controls, not only a visually plausible sequence.
open_questions: Which half was actually reversed in the quantitative benchmark, and were metrics computed against V1 or V1-prime?
How much of the reported gain remains when every method receives the same full-video observation and uses the same base generator?
Does the method outperform a full-video baseline using only target tracks, or are source tracks and source-background controls necessary?
How do interpolation, temporal resampling/reversal, and geometric transforms contribute separately to edit fidelity and preservation?
What is the success curve versus number of points, track overlap, trajectory length, displacement, occlusion duration, and number of independently moving objects?
Can 3D point tracks, depth, object masks, or camera decomposition resolve ambiguous 2D object-versus-camera edits without sacrificing the mask-free interface?
How sensitive are results to tracker choice and to injected tracking/visibility errors?
What jitter distribution best avoids copying while preserving pixel-level trajectory accuracy, and does jitter fail for very small objects?
How does identity, perceptual quality, and motion accuracy decay over repeated edits or longer-than-49-frame sequences?
Can the internal training data, derived pairs, prompts, and exact 100-video benchmark be released with licenses and preprocessing manifests?
What are the model's inference latency and memory, and how much user correction time is required for a successful edit?
Do blinded raters still prefer MotionV2V under preregistered random ordering, matched prompts, matched information, and confidence-interval reporting?

competitive_landscape.title: ReVideo: Remake a Video with Motion and Content Control
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct antecedent and paper-evaluated baseline for trajectory-guided video editing with separate motion and content controls.
competitive_landscape.difference: ReVideo starts from a reference/first frame and combines trajectory and content-region control, while MotionV2V consumes the complete source video and needs no user mask. This matters because MotionV2V's preservation advantage can come from observing later frames; a matched full-video comparison is required to attribute the gain to its method.

competitive_landscape.title: ATI: Any Trajectory Instruction for Controllable Video Generation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct trajectory-control competitor and the strongest user-study baseline reported by MotionV2V.
competitive_landscape.difference: ATI injects flexible object, local, and camera trajectories into an image-to-video model from a first frame, whereas MotionV2V defines a source-to-target trajectory delta over an existing full clip. ATI's lighter generative interface is broader for creation; MotionV2V's extra source evidence targets preservation and arbitrary-time editing.

competitive_landscape.title: Go-with-the-Flow: Motion-Controllable Video Diffusion Models Using Real-Time Warped Noise
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct motion-control competitor and paper-evaluated baseline using optical-flow-style warped diffusion noise.
competitive_landscape.difference: Go-with-the-Flow conditions generation through dense motion-warped noise and can retrofit pretrained video diffusion; MotionV2V uses sparse colored point correspondences plus the full source. The paper also changes Go-with-the-Flow's backbone to Wan2.2, so its reported comparison is an adaptation rather than a faithful controlled reproduction.

competitive_landscape.title: Motion Prompting: Controlling Video Generation with Motion Trajectories
competitive_landscape.relationship: Close antecedent for sparse and dense trajectory prompting of image-to-video generation and interactive motion manipulation.
competitive_landscape.difference: Motion Prompting controls generation from an image with trajectory prompts; MotionV2V edits an observed video's motion by pairing source and target tracks and retains content from all frames. The distinction is source-video editing versus image-conditioned generation, but the trajectory interface and control objective substantially overlap.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Video Motion Editing with 3D Point Tracks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Subsequent direct source-video motion editor using paired source and target point tracks.
competitive_landscape.difference: The later method lifts control into 3D tracks with explicit depth/occlusion reasoning and joint camera/object manipulation; MotionV2V uses simpler 2D rasterized correspondences and emphasizes arbitrary timestamp and temporal reversal. The later work narrows MotionV2V's claim to being the first or only point-track video-motion editor and exposes the importance of geometry-aware comparisons.

competitive_landscape.title: TRACE: Object Motion Editing in Videos with First-Frame Trajectory Guidance
competitive_landscape.relationship: Subsequent direct video-to-video competitor for changing object paths under source camera motion.
competitive_landscape.difference: TRACE converts an easy first-frame trajectory specification into frame-aligned boxes and focuses on object motion, while MotionV2V asks for sparse point correspondences across time and also targets camera and temporal edits. TRACE's narrower task may reduce user effort and handle camera motion more explicitly; MotionV2V offers a broader edit vocabulary.

competitive_landscape.title: TrajectoryMover: Generative Movement of Object Trajectories in Videos
competitive_landscape.relationship: Subsequent direct competitor for generative relocation of an object's trajectory in an existing video.
competitive_landscape.difference: TrajectoryMover builds a synthetic paired TrajectoryAtlas and edits the object's 3D relative trajectory, whereas MotionV2V constructs generic counterfactual motion pairs and uses 2D tracks for objects, camera, and time. Its explicit paired 3D formulation is a stronger comparator for object relocation; MotionV2V remains broader in edit type.

competitive_landscape.title: CamDirector: Towards Long-Term Coherent Video Trajectory Editing
competitive_landscape.relationship: Subsequent full-video trajectory editor specializing in camera motion and long-horizon consistency.
competitive_landscape.difference: CamDirector uses world caching and history-aware autoregression to edit camera trajectories over long videos; MotionV2V handles object, camera, and temporal edits but trains and evaluates short 49-frame clips without a long-term benchmark. It is therefore a narrower but materially stronger comparator for the camera-control and duration claims.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present MotionV2V as a new general video-motion editor that uses source-to-target point trajectories, full-video conditioning, and automatically generated counterfactual pairs to edit any object's motion from any timestamp while preserving the rest of the clip, without masks or per-video optimization.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The pinned paper demonstrates a distinctive combination of full-source conditioning, three rasterized source/target control videos, a frozen CogVideoX control branch, and interpolation/resampling/geometry-derived training pairs. Its 41-rater study and selected 100-video benchmark favor it over ATI, ReVideo, and Go-with-the-Flow, and examples cover object, camera, temporal, later-start, and iterative edits. However, no component ablation, matched-information baseline, reproducible quantitative construction, or broad failure-rate benchmark identifies which ingredient causes the gains.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest supported novelty is the integrated formulation of full-video 2D correspondence-delta editing plus scalable counterfactual-pair construction and an arbitrary-time interface. Sparse trajectory control itself, image-to-video motion prompting, content-aware video remaking, and warped-noise control are prior art. The claim of general superior preservation is weakened by first-frame-only baselines and a deliberately later-content test set; the exact quantitative pair is also ambiguous. Subsequent 3D-track, object-path, and long-horizon camera editors further narrow durable novelty to this particular broad 2D interface and data/architecture recipe rather than sole ownership of trajectory-based video motion editing.
